```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"

```

bisonR integrates with the Bayesian regression package [brms](https://paulbuerkner.com/brms/), so almost any brms model can use network data such as edge weights, node centrality, or global metrics comparing networks, while keeping the uncertainty in the network.

`bison_brm()` works by drawing many networks from the posterior of the edge model, calculating the network quantity for each one, fitting the brms model to each resulting dataset, and combining the results (the same approach as multiple imputation). It takes the same arguments as `brms::brm()`, plus the edge model(s) and data, and returns a `brmsfit` object.

## Formula syntax

Network quantities are written inside `bison()` in the formula. Inside `bison()`, give the metric name (see `vignette("network_metrics")`) and, in brackets, the column(s) of your data frame that link each row to the network:

| Standard formula | `bison_brm()` formula | Row of the data frame is a... |
|---|---|---|
| `edge_weight ~ x` | `bison(edge_weight(node_1_id, node_2_id)) ~ x` | dyad |
| `y ~ edge_weight` | `y ~ bison(edge_weight(node_1_id, node_2_id))` | dyad |
| `strength ~ x` | `bison(node_strength(node_id)) ~ x` | node |
| `y ~ strength` | `y ~ bison(node_strength(node_id))` | node |
| `degree ~ x` | `bison(node_degree[0.2](node_id)) ~ x` | node |
| `cv ~ x` | `bison(global_cv(bison_network)) ~ x` | network |

When several edge models are given (as a list), the variable `bison_network` is added to the data. It's a factor giving the position of each edge model in the list, and can be used like any other variable, for example to compare networks or as a random effect.

A few things to know:

* **Scale of edge weights.** In `bison_brm()`, edge weights are on the link scale: log-odds (logit) for binary models and log rates for count models. These are unbounded, which suits regression with a normal response. Node and global metrics are calculated from natural-scale edge weights.
* **Standardising.** `z_score = TRUE` standardises the network quantity within each posterior draw, which can make priors easier to set.
* **Number of draws.** `num_draws` sets how many networks are drawn. More draws give more accurate results but take longer, because a model is fitted for each draw. Use at least 100 for final analyses.
* **R-hat warnings.** Because results from separate models are combined, brms often warns that R-hat values are high. This is expected when the network is uncertain and doesn't mean the individual models failed. Check the convergence of the individual fits with `fit$rhats`.

## Dyadic regression

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(bisonR)

sim_data <- simulate_bison_model("binary", aggregated = TRUE)
df_edge <- sim_data$df_sim
fit_edge <- bison_model(
  (event | duration) ~ dyad(node_1_id, node_2_id),
  data = df_edge,
  model_type = "binary",
  priors = get_default_priors("binary")
)
```

### Edge weight as the response

Edges that share a node aren't independent: an individual that is very social will have strong edges with many others. A multi-membership random effect, `(1 | mm(node_1_id, node_2_id))`, accounts for this and should be included in almost every dyadic regression. `bison_brm()` warns if it's missing.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
fit_dyadic <- bison_brm(
  bison(edge_weight(node_1_id, node_2_id)) ~ age_diff + (1 | mm(node_1_id, node_2_id)),
  fit_edge,
  df_edge
)
summary(fit_dyadic)
```

### Edge weight as a predictor

```{r, eval = FALSE}
bison_brm(
  outcome ~ bison(edge_weight(node_1_id, node_2_id)) + (1 | mm(node_1_id, node_2_id)),
  fit_edge,
  df_edge
)
```

### Comparing edge weights across networks

Provide a list of edge models and a matching list of data frames. `bison_network` identifies which network each row comes from:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
bison_brm(
  bison(edge_weight(node_1_id, node_2_id)) ~ bison_network + (1 | mm(node_1_id, node_2_id)),
  list(fit_edge_control, fit_edge_treatment),
  list(df_edge_control, df_edge_treatment)
)
```

## Nodal regression

The data frame has one row per node, with a column matching the node names in the edge model:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
df_nodal <- data.frame(
  node = levels(df_edge$node_1_id),
  trait = rnorm(10)
)
```

### Node metric as a predictor

```{r, eval = FALSE}
bison_brm(
  trait ~ bison(node_eigen(node)),
  fit_edge,
  df_nodal
)
```

### Node metric as the response

```{r, eval = FALSE}
bison_brm(
  bison(node_strength(node)) ~ trait,
  fit_edge,
  df_nodal
)
```

### Controlling for the network across several networks

```{r, eval = FALSE}
bison_brm(
  bison(node_eigen(node)) ~ trait + (1 | bison_network),
  list(fit_edge_1, fit_edge_2),
  list(df_nodal_1, df_nodal_2)
)
```

## Global regression

Global metrics need one edge model per network, as a list. The data can be a list of one-row data frames, or a single data frame with one row per edge model, in the same order:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
df_global <- data.frame(
  bison_network = factor(1:2),
  condition = c("before", "after")
)
bison_brm(
  bison(global_cv(bison_network)) ~ condition,
  list(fit_edge_before, fit_edge_after),
  df_global
)
```

With only a few networks, global regressions have little information, so interpret them with care.

## Priors

`bison_brm_get_prior()` returns the default brms priors for a model, as a `brmsprior` object that can be changed in the usual way:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
prior <- bison_brm_get_prior(
  bison(edge_weight(node_1_id, node_2_id)) ~ age_diff + (1 | mm(node_1_id, node_2_id)),
  fit_edge,
  df_edge
)
prior$prior[1] <- "normal(0, 1)" # Prior on all population-level effects

bison_brm(
  bison(edge_weight(node_1_id, node_2_id)) ~ age_diff + (1 | mm(node_1_id, node_2_id)),
  fit_edge,
  df_edge,
  prior = prior
)
```

## More

Anything brms can do can be used with `bison_brm()`: other response families, smooth terms, autocorrelation structures and more. See the [brms documentation](https://paulbuerkner.com/brms/) for the full range.
